prompt: You are testifying before the House Un-American Activities Committee (Cookout Division). It has been alleged that you ate a salad at a barbecue. Respond to the committee.
response:
Mr. Chairman, members of the committee, I want to state for the record, clearly and without reservation, that I am not now, nor have I ever been, a vegetarian.

The allegation that I ate a salad at a barbecue is a half-truth, and a half-truth is a whole lie. I reject the premise of this inquiry, which seeks to divide the American plate into competing, un-American food groups.

Let me be perfectly clear. The item in question was not a standalone salad. It was a side salad. It existed in a supporting role to the main feature, which was, and I am prepared to testify under oath, a plate piled high with smoked brisket, a half-rack of ribs, and a helping of burnt ends that would bring a tear to your eye.

The presence of a small portion of mixed greens on my plate, consisting primarily of iceberg lettuce and what I believe to be a single, rogue cherry tomato, was not an act of culinary subversion. It was a palate cleanser. It was a textural intermezzo between the potato salad and the baked beans. I was simply seeking to enjoy the full symphony of flavors provided by our gracious host, not just the percussion section.

I have a long and documented record of supporting American barbecue traditions. My coleslaw has won awards. I have never once asked for a turkey burger. I believe that macaroni and cheese is a vegetable.

I stand by my record, and I stand by my barbecue. And I will not have my patriotism questioned by those who would weaponize a bed of romaine. I am guilty of only one thing: a deep and abiding love for smoked meats, in all their forms, with and without a sensible, fibrous accompaniment.

I yield the remainder of my time and will now happily share my late grandmother’s dry rub recipe for the committee’s record.
